opening: You did not spend the last of it on yourself. That was a decision, made late and made fast, and it was yours to make.

clauses.text: You went down at your own door, on the side of it where the work had been done.
The walls had turned it away before — more than once, on nights nobody was awake to count. They did not owe you another one.
They had come through those walls once already, and taken the place off you, and you had gone on anyway — which is the part of it worth remembering.
Inside there were rooms you had made mean something — a place to cook, a place to keep water, a place that was not just out of the rain.
The work you had started was still standing half-done behind you, close enough that anyone coming after could see what it was going to be.
You had held that address for days by then, which in what is left of this city is a long tenancy.
You did not go quietly and it was not cheap for them.
Nothing you did to keep that door shut was anything you would have needed to lie about afterwards.
You had done harder things than this to keep that door shut, and at the end it was the door that mattered to you, not the things.
There was somebody behind you when it took you, and you held long enough for that to have been the point of it.
There was nobody behind you. You stood in it anyway.
You picked a spot and you did not come off it, and that is a smaller thing than it sounds and a larger one than it looks.
You never had an address in this city. It turned out you did not need one to have something left worth spending.
You were only ever here a couple of days. You still found something at the end of them worth putting yourself between.
You had walked half this city without once stopping anywhere long enough to call it yours, and then you stopped for good, on purpose, in a doorway that was nobody's.
You had covered a lot of this city by then — more of it than most people ever see of the one they live in — and you spent the end of it standing still.
You had gone through building after building until there was nothing left in them, and you finished with nothing on you that was going to help.
The mass had rolled over you more than once already and you had got up both times. The third time you did not try.
By then the city had taken almost everyone in it who had a name. You were not the first and you had stopped expecting to be the last.
You had not had to become anything you would rather not be, and at the end you did not start.
There were things you had done to get this far that you would not have wanted read out. The last one was not among them.
Four days, five, however many it had been — long enough that stopping was a decision and not just what happened next.
